title: A Storm of Light
caption: The galaxy NGC 4495, imaged by the Dark Energy Camera on the Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope
credit: Dark Energy Survey/DOE/FNAL/DECam/CTIO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA · Image processing: Travis Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage/NSF NOIRLab), Jen Miller (Gemini Observatory/NSF NOIRLab), Mahdi Zamani & Davide de Martin (NSF NOIRLab)

recognition.text: NOIRLab Image of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: NGC 4495 lies in the constellation Coma Berenices, which hosts myriad other astronomical objects. It has had a turbulent past: astronomers have recorded several supernovae there over the years, including three named 1994S, 2010lo and 2011ca.

Those explosions did not all happen the same way. 1994S was a Type Ia supernova, set off when a white dwarf, the leftover core of a star, interacted with a companion star and its core reignited. 2011ca was a Type Ic supernova, which happens when the core of a single massive star collapses. A supernova is a dying star's final burst of energy, and several different processes can trigger one.

The image was taken with the Department of Energy's Dark Energy Camera (DECam), working on the Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope in Chile, as part of the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys. Those surveys blended three projects that together observed a third of the night sky.

explore: The Legacy Surveys were carried out to choose targets for the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), an international collaboration managed by the Department of Energy's Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. Most of the money to build and run DESI comes from the DOE's Office of Science.
